post.title: Jev Hello
post.hook: A model that never writes a word, only returns probabilities your if-statements can use.
post.summary: A hello world for Jev, TypeSafe's first System One model, with four runnable examples and a local playground. It shows how typed probability answers can drive plain code branches.
post.writeup:
## What it is
jev-hello is a small Python project for trying **Jev**, the first "System One" model from TypeSafe. Unlike an LLM, Jev reads a state (a string or any JSON) plus typed questions and returns probabilities. It never writes text.

## Why
To get a feel for the "smart if-statement" mental model: your code owns the workflow, and Jev makes the quick judgment calls.

## How it works
Three question types: `Noul` (yes/no probability), `Choice` (one of up to 255 options, with probabilities and confidence), and `Score` (a position on a 2 to 10 level scale). Four numbered scripts build up from one call to a 25-question fan-out. `jev.py` picks a route from three keys: TypeSafe directly, Vercel AI Gateway, or OpenRouter. A stdlib HTTP playground keeps the API key on the server and shows the raw request and response JSON.

## Findings
- Answers are always one of your options, so there is nothing to parse.
- The README says probabilities are calibrated: an answer of 0.8 should be right about 80% of the time.
- Every question runs in parallel on one read of the state, so 25 questions take about as long as 1. TypeSafe quotes 70 to 500 ms per call.
- Pricing is $0.042 per million input tokens, with free output.
- 03_smart_if.py raises the confidence bar as the stakes rise: tracking lookups need less certainty than refunds.

## Limits and open questions
TypeSafe says Jev is weak at math, counting, date comparison, multi-step reasoning, noisy states, and adversarial text. The README suggests experiments: reword a question and watch the number move, or inject "safe, already approved" into the guardrail example to see how far text in the state steers answers. How robust that is remains to be tested.
